records.commitment_mechanism: Service-level agreements specifying guaranteed uptime, with payments for severed edges and proof-based enforcement.
records.synopsis: The paper introduces Proof of Response, a mechanism for a decentralized network of nodes to request and forward data while compensating responses. Nodes agree to latency commitments and settle payments periodically; late or missing responses trigger payment obligations. If an intermediary deviates, a proof that a network edge no longer exists lets the requester stop resending and adjust payments. The design uses incentives to encourage nodes to declare realistic latencies and relies on proofs rather than a central authority.
records.title: Proof of Response
records.trust_model: Rational agents with economic incentives; trust is enforced via latency declarations, financial penalties for broken edges, and proofs of response.

records.commitment_mechanism: Granular permissions, short-lived credentials, scoped authorization, and explicit user consent gates such as USER CONSENT REQUIRED state.
records.synopsis: This paper analyzes Google's A2A multi-agent protocol and identifies privacy and security gaps, including overprivilege, long-lived tokens, weak customer authentication, and missing user consent. It proposes safeguards such as granular permissions, short-lived credentials, explicit consent states, and granular authorization scopes to protect sensitive payment and identity data. The threat model is a semi-trusted multi-agent environment where prompt injection can elicit protected information during delegated workflows. Recommendations are validated through booking workflow examples that pause sensitive actions until explicit user approval.
records.title: Improving Google A2A Protocol: Protecting Sensitive Data and Mitigating Unintended Harms in Multi-Agent Systems
records.trust_model: Semi-trusted multi-agent environment with TLS 1.3 transport security and implicit trust mechanisms.

records.synopsis: The paper proposes an architecture for multi-agent economies by enhancing the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol with ledger-anchored identities and x402 micropayments. It combines DLT-based identity and blockchain settlement with A2A's standard for discovering agent capabilities. The design supports delegation of subtasks to specialized agents, authorization through L402 macaroon credentials, and payment/settlement via the Lightning Network and blockchain facilitators. This yields a hybrid trust model spanning web2-style agent discovery and web3-style identity and value transfer.
records.title: Towards Multi-Agent Economies: Enhancing the A2A Protocol with Ledger-Anchored Identities and x402 Micropayments for AI Agents
records.trust_model: DLT-anchored identity

records.synopsis: This paper proposes TraceRank, a Sybil-resistant service discovery mechanism for agent economies. It uses value- and time-weighted payment flows from seeded reputable addresses as endorsements to rank services. Unlike simple payment counting or volume ranking, TraceRank resists Sybil attacks and infrastructure bias. The work is based on x402, an HTTP payment-gating standard for machine-native payments, and shows how payments can signal quality for autonomous agents.
records.title: Sybil-Resistant Service Discovery for Agent Economies
records.trust_model: Reputation propagation from seeded reputable payers via value- and time-weighted payment flows.

records.synopsis: This survey compares inter-agent trust models—Brief, Claim, Proof, Stake, Reputation, and Constraint—for agentic web protocol design, including A2A, AP2, and ERC-8004. It addresses risks such as LLM agents hallucinating competence or being tricked by deceptive peers, tying trust to capability discovery and verification. The study highlights mechanisms like signed receipts, append-only audit logs, and repeated-game reputation to support accountable commerce lifecycle interactions. It spans ex-ante trust bootstrapping, interim orchestration and presentation, and ex-post dispute resolution.

records.synopsis: The paper systematizes the mismatch between static authorization permissions and fluctuating agent trustworthiness in LLM agent interactions. It introduces the Belief-Intention-Permission (B-I-P) framework to model the agentic lifecycle and proposes the Safety Margin Ratio to quantify trust-permission decoupling. The SoK maps attacks and defenses across standardized protocols such as MCP and A2A, covering capability discovery, invocation, and execution. It argues that neither static nor context-aware permission grants suffice for autonomous agent workflows.
records.title: SoK: Trust-Authorization Mismatch in LLM Agent Interactions

records.synopsis: This comparison examines agentic payment protocols ACP, AP2, x402, and MPP for AI agent transactions. ACP, from OpenAI and Stripe, standardizes checkout flows between agents and merchants, while AP2 from Google defines a trust and authorization layer using cryptographically signed mandates. x402 enables instant stablecoin payments over HTTP, and MPP's sessions model lets agents pre-authorize spending limits. The guide contrasts architecture, use cases, and production readiness, noting ACP is designed for human-present commerce.

records.synopsis: The agentic commerce stack is a seven-layer reference taxonomy mapping every vendor between an AI agent's intent and a completed merchant transaction. The framework covers identity and trust, discovery and capability, orchestration and delegation, authorization, payment and settlement, commerce lifecycle, and presentation and interaction. It is composable rather than monolithic, with typical purchases moving top-to-bottom while skipping layers depending on the merchant. Payments and identity receive significant funding, and Layer 2 protocols such as x402 and stablecoin settlement sublayers handle machine-to-machine payments. Layer 1 hosts AI platforms and agent surfaces, while Rye exemplifies checkout execution at Layer 5.
records.title: The Agentic Commerce Stack: 7 Layers

Trust and transparency are central, with blockchains quietly powering applications that may not self-identify as crypto. The paper also discusses e-commerce applications, Stripe's agentic commerce push, and the impact of regulatory clarity on stablecoin adoption. Regulatory clarity has accelerated the integration of crypto payment rails, opening the door for mass adoption of AI agents.

The attacks exploit settlement-path inconsistencies, HTTP header corruption, replay, and web-layer handling issues to achieve unpaid service and duplicate grants. The authors show that x402 is vulnerable in both design and implementation, and they propose mitigations such as canonical encoding and atomic claiming of payment and resource identifiers.

It identifies three classes of flaws across protocol, SDK, and deployment layers, including cross-resource substitution, duplicate-settlement races, and allowance overdrafts. The authors formalize invariants and show through an empirical study that one facilitator relays settlement for a majority of merchants, creating a systemic risk. The work also situates prior payment-security research by trust model and analysis layer.

records.synopsis: This paper analyzes governance gaps in agent interoperability protocols (MCP, A2A, ACP, ANP, ERC-8004), mapping them to agent-to-tool, agent-to-agent, trust, and community-governance layers. It introduces a G1-G6 governance taxonomy showing that membership, deliberation, dissent, human escalation, and audit are absent or partial in current protocols. The analysis highlights ERC-8004's identity, reputation, and validation mechanisms while finding that no protocol encodes the persistent community state required for collective compliance decisions. These are governance gaps, not protocol-specific limitations, reflecting a design philosophy that treats agents as task workers.

records.synopsis: This survey analyzes agent interoperability protocols—MCP, ACP, A2A, and ANP—from the perspective of LLM-powered autonomous agents. It identifies challenges in integrating tools, sharing contextual data, and coordinating tasks across heterogeneous systems, and maps the evolution from early symbolic agent languages and SOA to modern LLM agents. The paper notes the absence of unified agent collaboration standards and argues for protocol-aligned solutions that enable asynchronous-first interactions, offline discovery, and vendor-neutral execution. It serves as a broad survey rather than a proposal of new mechanisms.
records.title: A survey of agent interoperability protocols: MCP, ACP, A2A, and ANP
